Effect of aeration pretreatment on anaerobic digestion of swine manure
Juan Wanga, Xindong Wanga,b, Chunlin Biana,b, Jianguo Liuc and Benyi Xiao 
b
aCollege of Civil Engineering, Inner Mongolia University of Technology, Hohhot, People’s Republic of China; bResearch Center for Eco–

ABSTRACT  
To investigate the effects of aeration pretreatment on the anaerobic digestion (AD) of swine 
manure, five pretreatment groups were established with dissolved oxygen (DO) in each group 
set to 0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.4, and 2.0 mg/L, respectively. The results demonstrated that compared to 
the non-aeration group, methane production increased to varying degrees with different 
aeration pretreatments (AP), with a maximum increase of 27.98% (DO = 2.0 mg/L). AP reduced 
the hydrogen sulfide (H2S) content of biogas. The H2S concentration in the DO = 2.0 mg/L was 
only 0.209%, and this represented an increased H2S removal rate of 49.27% compared to that of 
the DO = 0.0 mg/L (0.412%). Simultaneously, AP increases the hydrolysis rate. When the DO 
concentration reached 2.0 mg/L, the hydrolysis rate reached its maximum. An increase in the 
hydrolysis rate further enhanced the removal rate of organic matter. The organic matter 
removal rate was highest (36.96%) at DO = 2.0 mg/L. AP effectively prolonged the methane 
generation time and shortened the lag time of methane generation. AP creates a brief micro 
aerobic environment, accelerates substrate hydrolysis, and promotes the production and 
consumption of total volatile fatty acids, particularly acetic acid. Additionally, AP promoted the 
symbiotic relationship between Caldicoprobacter (20.93%–34.96%) and Metanosaeta (14.73%– 
18.45%).

1. Introduction
With increasing demand for meat, eggs, and dairy pro­
ducts, the livestock industry has developed rapidly in 
recent years. Pork is a major source of human food, 
accounting for over 40% of the total meat consumed 
worldwide [1]. The rapid development of pig farming 
has produced large amount of manure, and swine 
manure (SM) contains large amounts of organic 
matter, nitrogen, and phosphorus. If not handled and 
stacked properly, it can cause environmental pollution, 
affect human health, and can easily cause eutrophica­
tion of water bodies when discharged into water [2,3]. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) provides a new method for 
treating SM and is an important technology for 
organic waste treatment and biomass energy utilisation. 
AD protects the environment and reduces pollutants 
while reducing the use of fossil energy using the pro­
duced biogas as a fuel, and the digestate can be used 
as an organic fertiliser for agricultural production, thus 
facilitating the recycling of resources and energy [4].

Despite the merits mentioned above, AD of SM pos­
sesses several drawbacks, such as a low hydrolysis rate, 
toxic hydrogen sulfide (H2S) release, and poor system 
stability. Previous studies demonstrated that microaera­
tion can overcome these issues. Traditionally, AD 
systems have been maintained in a strictly anaerobic 
environment, as oxygen inhibits the activity of specific 
anaerobic microorganisms and methanogens [5]. 
However, it was recently reported that introducing a 
small amount of air or oxygen into the digester can 
accelerate the AD reaction rate, increase methane 
yield, promote substrate degradation, and reduce the 
H2S content of biogas [6,7]. However, due to its sensi­
tivity to changes in equipment and internal material 
conditions [8,9], direct long-term and excessive oxygen­
ation also damages the stability of anaerobic systems, 
ultimately leading to higher energy consumption. Aera­
tion pretreatment (AP) of AD raw materials can effec­
tively avoid these problems. As AP is performed 
outside the digester, it is often more convenient, does 
not affect the activity of methanogens, and does not 
damage the airtightness of the digester.
Previous studies have investigated the effect of AP on 
the AD of sewage sludge and olive factory wastewater 
and observed that AP can enhance the hydrolysis of 
organic matter, increase the methane yield and 
organic matter removal in AD, boost enzyme activity, 
and reduce the concentration of H2S. Rashvanlou et al. 
[10] observed through AD of sewage sludge that AP 
(0.2 Lair/Lliquid/min [vvm] for 40 h) increased the soluble 
chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) by 65% and key 
enzyme activity by 10%. Jenícek et al. [11] conducted 
AD of municipal sludge in an engineering application 
(3,000 m3) and observed that AP (1.2 m3/h) could 
remove up to 99.5% of the H2S from biogas. Alrawash­
deh et al. [12] reported that AP (0.5 vvm for 4 days) 
can improve the removal rates of volatile solids (VS) 
(56%) and total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) 
(70%) and increase biogas yield by 111% during the 
AD of olive factory wastewater. Meanwhile, to optimise 
AP, previous studies have also investigated the effect 
of AP parameters such as intensity, time, and tempera­
ture on AD [13]. For example, Montalvo et al. [13] com­
pared the effects of different AP Aintensities, time, and 
temperatures on AD of sewage sludge and observed 
that AP increased the concentrations of soluble proteins, 
soluble polysaccharides, and SCOD, and improved the 
removal rate of VS with the optimal AP parameters as 
0.3 vvm, 48 h, and 35 °C. Although most previous 
studies used the aeration rate (vvm) to represent AP 
intensity, the dissolved oxygen (DO) level was not deter­
mined, and this approach cannot reveal the DO level of 
the pretreated solution and the actual oxygen 
concentration that contacts the organic matter and 
microorganisms. Aeration rates often are different for 
different equipment and environments. Additionally, it 
remains unclear whether AP affects biochemical pro­
cesses other than hydrolysis in AD, and the study of 
dynamic models remains in the exploratory stage [14].
Therefore, this study explored the effect of AP on the 
AD of SM by setting different DO levels. Dynamic models 
were used to reveal the effects of AP on the four main 
AD steps (hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and 
methanogenesis). It hopes that this study provides a 
reference for the improvement of AD in the context of 
SM.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Feedstock and inoculum
The SM used in this study was obtained from a pig farm 
in Beijing, China, and the inoculum was sludge obtained 
from a laboratory anaerobic digester. All materials were 
sampled on site, and the manure was hand-picked to 
remove visible weeds and gravel particles. It was 
mixed well, and some samples were then used to test 
their basic physicochemical properties. The remaining 
samples were stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C. AD 
sludge was used as the inoculum, and its basic physico­
chemical properties were tested. The basic physico­
chemical properties of the experimental materials are 
presented in Table 1.
2.2. Aeration pretreatment
The AP of SM was carried out in a 1 L reactor (working 
volume 0.65 L). SM and inoculum were first mixed at a 
ratio of 1:3 (v/v) in the reactor, and the pH of the 
mixture was adjusted to 7.5 ± 0.1 using 0.1 M HCl. A 
1.5 W aeration pump (AquaBlue, China) with 0.3 vvm 
was then used, and a DO meter was used to monitor

2.3. Batch anaerobic digestion
Batch AD was conducted in laboratory-scale testing to 
evaluate the effect of APs (DO = 0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.4, and 
2.0 mg/L) on the CH4 yield of SM. The digesters 
were placed in a constant temperature water bath at 
37±1 °C and stirred at 150 rpm. The batch ADs lasted 
for 36 days.
2.4. Chemical analysis
Biogas production was measured by collecting the drai­
nage gas. The methane content of the biogas was 
detected using a gas chromatograph (GC) (Agilent 
6890N, USA) equipped with a flame ionisation detector 
(FID) and a 30 m capillary column (HP-5). The H2S 
content of the biogas was determined using a GC 
(Agilent 6890N, USA) equipped with an FID and a 30 m 
capillary column (DB-1701). The total sulfur content of 
the digestive products was monitored using an organic 
element analyzer (Elementar Rapid cs Cube, Germany). 
Sulfur-containing samples were placed in quartz com­
bustion tubes using an automatic sampler. Under the 
catalysis of tungsten trioxide oxidation at a high temp­
erature of 1150 °C and the driving force of oxygen 
carrier gas, all sulfur elements were converted into 
sulfur dioxide. After drying, it entered an infrared detec­
tor, and the sulfur content was determined by monitor­
ing the sulfur dioxide concentration. Another GC 
(Agilent 6890N, USA) equipped with an FID was used 
to detect the volatile fatty acids (VFAs). The total and 
soluble indices of the digestate samples were deter­
mined. The samples for the analysis of soluble items 
were centrifuged at 8,000 rpm for 30 min and then 
passed through 0.45 μm filters prior to analysis. The 
digestate pH was measured using a pH meter 
(BANTE900, Shanghai Special Instruments Factory). 
Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), proteins, carbo­
hydrates, ammonia nitrogen (TAN), and COD of the 
digestates samples were determined according to 
standard methods [15]. The digestates were sampled 
at 36 days to analyze the microbial community (bacteria 
and archaea) using a method similar to that used in 
previous studies [16].

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Gas indicators
3.1.1. Biogas production
In the AP AD experiments, various gas yield indicators of 
each group were compared to those of the control 
group to provide a comprehensive analysis of the 
effect of different oxygen contents on digestion. The 
daily gas yield, cumulative gas yield, methane content, 
and cumulative methane yield of the digestion units 
with different oxygen contents are presented in Figure 1.
In the AD experiment with AP, the DO level exerted a 
significant impact on gas yield and reaction stability 
throughout the AD process. Overall, the main purpose 
of the pretreatment was to increase the methane yield, 
accelerate the AD process, and improve the substrate 
degradation rate. Cumulative methane yield was calcu­
lated from the first day of AD until no significant gas 
yield was detected. From Figure 1(a) it could be 
observed that the gas yield of the five groups of the 
experiment rose faster on the first day, among which, 
the gas yield of the DO = 0.4 mg/L group reached 
9.53 mL/g VS/d. This was followed by the DO = 0.8 mg/ 
L group with a gas yield of 7.72 mL/g VS/d, likely due 
to the heat expansion of the gas in the digestion tank 
and the increase in gas pressure in the digestion tank 
that primarily represented the hydrolysis stage of the 
AD process at this time. The concentration of methane 
in the produced gas was low, as presented in Figure 1
(c). The methane content increased rapidly after day 5, 
when the more easily hydrolysed sugars in the digester 
were partially decomposed and utilised by anaerobic 
bacteria and when methanogens began to grow. The 
reaction began, and the daily gas yield of each group 
gradually increased, reaching its peak on the 23rd day 
before rapidly decreasing thereafter. Daily methane 
yield exhibited the same trend. The small amount of 
gas produced in the early stages of the reaction may 
be related to the activity of the inoculum, which also 
possesses the potential to increased gas yield. As the 
reaction progressed, a large amount of VFAs was pro­
duced during the acidification stage, and the gas yield

By comparing the effects of different DO levels on

increased with increasing DO concentration. However, 
after the DO concentration reached a certain level, its 
effect on the gas yield gradually decreased. For 
example, the DO = 2.0 mg/L group exhibited the 
highest cumulative methane yield but only increased 
by 1.86% compared to that of the DO = 1.4 mg/L 
group. The results indicated that the impact of 
different DO levels on the methane yield in the AD of 
SM varied. This may be due to the observation that all 
APs enhance the hydrolysis of organic matter, boost 
enzyme activity, and reduce the inhibition of H2S, TAN, 
and VFAs by lowering their concentrations with 
different effects [24–27]. Therefore, when aeration is 
used as a pretreatment method for the AD process, 
the amount of aeration must be strictly controlled, as 
excessive oxygen may inhibit the activity of methano­
gens and further reduce the methane yield, even 
affecting the stable operation of the AD system [26]. 
Moreover, excessive oxygen might oxidise certain sub­
stances required by methanogens (such as VFAs) or 
aerobic methane oxidising bacteria might consume 
methane.

3.1.2. H2s content
H2S formation is a challenging problem that occurs 
during AD, and the effects of different DO levels on 
H2S formation were assessed (Figure 2). In the DO =  
0.0 mg/L group, the H2S concentration increased 
sharply at the beginning of the reaction. As the DO 
level increased, the appearance of H2S in the biogas 
exhibited varying degrees of delay. The H2S production 
time in the DO = 0.4, 0.8, 1.4, and 2.0 mg/L groups was 
delayed by 1, 2, 4, and 6 days, respectively, compared 
to that of the control group. At the end of the reaction, 
the H2S content in each group of biogas remained stable 
at 0.412% (DO = 0.0 mg/L), 0.349% (DO = 0.4 mg/L), 
0.306% (DO = 0.8 mg/L), 0.234% (DO = 1.4 mg/L), and 
0.209% (DO = 2.0 mg/L), respectively. Compared to the 
DO = 0.0 mg/L group, AP reduced the H2S content 
from 15.29% (DO = 0.4 mg/L) to 49.27% (DO = 2.0 mg/ 
L), with the DO = 2.0 mg/L group exhibiting the best 
H2S removal effect. The results revealed that the concen­
tration of H2S in the biogas decreased as the DO levels 
increased, indicating that oxygen effectively reduced 
the H2S content in the biogas. This was similar to the 
results of previous research [28]. Sulfate reducing bac­
teria (SRB) reduce methane yield by competing for 
various organic and inorganic substrates (acetate, buty­
rate, fatty acids, hydrogen, and propionate) [29]. At pH 
7–8, the generated H2S is toxic to methane-producing 
bacteria, thus further inhibiting methane yield [24]. 
Therefore, the removal of H2S reduces the inhibition of 
H2S on methanogens and increases methane yield [30].
The effects of different DO levels on the concen­
tration of sulfides in the matrix were different. The 
total sulfur concentration in the digested material was 
measured at the beginning and end of the test (Table 
3). The results indicated that when DO = 0.0 mg/L, the 
total sulfur concentration in the termination sample 
was the lowest. As the DO levels increased, the total 
sulfur concentration in the digester also increased, ulti­
mately reaching a maximum value of 4.445 mg/g in 
the DO = 2.0 mg/L group. AP exerts a significant 
impact on the biological and chemical processes of 
sulfides in substrates. During the traditional AD 
process, SRB reduced sulfur compounds in the substrate 
to H2S in the form of biogas and sulfides in the liquid 
phase (HS−, S2−). H2S is the product of sulfur reduction 
by the SRB. The addition of trace amounts of oxygen 
to the digester directly inhibited sulfate reduction and 
reduced the production of H2S. In contrast, SRB were 
inhibited after AP, whereas sulfate-oxidising bacteria 
(SOB) proliferated in large numbers, further retaining 
sulfur-containing compounds in the biogas slurry. The 
overall biological desulfurisation reaction in the pres­
ence of SOB is as follows [30]:

3.2.1. Effect on pH and TAN
Samples were taken every two days during the reaction 
to measure the pH (Figure 3(a)). The low concentration 
of inoculum and low numbers of methanogens during 
the first 4 days of the reaction process resulted in 
limited use of the VFAs produced by acid-producing 
bacteria hydrolysis and led to an accumulation of 
VFAs, at which time the pH of the reaction system 
decreased, with the lowest pH in the DO = 2.0 mg/L 
group falling to 7.26 on day 9. However, as the high 
nitrogen content of SM was supplemented with NH4
+-N 
formed by hydrolysis, which could neutralise the acid 
produced to some extent, the pH drop at the beginning 
of the reaction did not inhibit the growth of methano­
gens. Thereafter, as the methanogens grew and multi­
plied, their ability to use VFAs to produce methane 
increased, and the daily methane concentration and 
gas yield increased. At this time, the pH rose rapidly, 
after which the VFAs produced by hydrolysis and acidifi­
cation no longer accumulated until the end of the reac­
tion, when the pH was finally stabilised at approximately 
7.90. The pH remained stable between 7.26 and 7.92 
throughout the reaction.
During AD, nitrogen is an important nutrient for 
microbial growth and reproduction, and the TAN exhi­
bits a buffering capacity in the fermentation system. 
However, excessive nitrogen content in anaerobic fer­
mentation substrates can inhibit microbial activity and 
reduce the biogas yield. In the AD of SM, the inhibitory 
concentration of TAN was 3,500–3,800 mg/L, and the 
process was blocked at 2,300–2,400 mg/L [25]. Figure 3
(b) show the changes in TAN inside each digester 
under different AP conditions. Different DO levels 
exerted a significant impact on the changes in TAN 
during the AD of SM. After the AP, the TAN concen­
trations of mixtures were reduced from 831.29 mg/L to 
379.40 mg/L when the DO levels increased from 
0.0 mg/L to 2.0 mg/L. During AD, the TAN concentration 
gradually increased and stabilised at the end of the test 
(Figure 3). The results demonstrated that the DO level of 
APs affected the TAN concentration with a higher DO 
level and a lower concentration of TAN, indicating that 
the DO levels reduced the inhibition of TAN (particularly 
free ammonia; FAN) and enhanced methane yield.
AP positively impacts the biological and chemical 
processes that alleviate ammonia inhibition in the AD 
of SM. In an aqueous solution, TAN exists in two forms 
including NH4
+-N and FAN. AP significantly enhanced 
the early degradation of proteins and released NH4
+-N 
and FAN into the SM. NH4
+-N, as a buffering substance, 
could effectively prevent acid inhibition during AD. Ni 
et al. [31] demonstrated that appropriate AP in AD 
could improve organic matter removal efficiency and 
provide a buffer to neutralise the excess VFAs produced. 
FAN is the main ammonia component inhibiting anaero­
bic fermentation. As NH3 is prone to volatilisation in 
aqueous solutions, gas (carrier gas) was introduced 
into the fermentation solution to fully contact the fer­
mentation broth and allow NH3 to pass through the 
gas–liquid interface and transfer to the gas phase, 
thereby achieving the removal of TAN.

Figure 10(a) presents the correlation between bac­
terial genera and environmental factors. Clostridium 
Sensu Stricto 1 was positively correlated with the concen­
trations of various organic compounds (including TCOD, 
SCOD, and VFAs) and TAN. This indicated that Clostri­
dium Sensu Stricto 1 possessed strong hydrolytic activity 
and good tolerance towards substrates and that organic 
acids and TAN may promote an increase in its relative 
abundance. Caldicobacter positively correlated with 
methane yield and organic matter removal efficiency. 
This indicated that Caldicobacter could fully utilise the 
hydrolysed products and achieve substance conversion. 
Additionally, Caldicobacter is more suitable for living in 
environments with high DO levels and is more sensitive 
to inhibitors (VFAs and TAN). Therefore, the abundance 
of Caldicobacter increased significantly after AP. Accord­
ing to previous reports, Caldicobacter was the dominant 
microorganism in AD systems and plays an important 
role in biogas yield [45].
Figure 10(b) presents the correlation between the 
archaeal genera and environmental factors. Methanosaeta 
exhibits a strong positive correlation with methane yield, 
DO levels, and pH. This result indicates that Methanosaeta 
was the main methane-producing archaea and had a high 
tolerance to oxygen. However, Methanosaeta was signifi­
cantly and negatively correlated with VFAs and TAN, indi­
cating poor stability and susceptibility to inhibition. This 
was similar to the results of previous research [46]. Metha­
nobacterium was significantly correlated with TAN and 
VFAs but negatively correlated with DO levels. This indi­
cated that Methanobacterium possessed strong adapta­
bility to ammonia inhibition and acid inhibition; 
however its activity decreased at high oxygen concen­
trations. Therefore, Methanobacterium was highly abun­
dant in all experimental groups but exhibited a 
decreasing trend with increasing DO levels. A similar 
finding was reported by Cheng et al. [47], who demon­
strated that the methanogens in the AP group were pri­
marily Methanosarcina, whereas those in the non- 
pretreatment group were primarily Methanobacterium.
The RDA results were consistent with the composition 
and distribution of microbial genera, thus indicating that 
environmental factors had a significant impact on the 
distribution of microbial communities. In practical appli­
cations, it is necessary to control key environmental 
factors to obtain an efficient methane-producing 
microbial community structure and enhance the 
methane yield potential of the substrates.
4. Conclusions
Microaerobic bacteria improved methane yield during 
SM batch experiments by regulating the microbial 
community structure. Facultative bacteria were capable 
of secreting hydrolytic enzymes and were stimulated 
by oxygen, leading to more rapid hydrolysis and 
higher VFA yield. Methanogens with oxygen tolerance 
were also enriched. This study demonstrated the ben­
eficial effects of AP on batch AD of SM, which could 
also provide a reference for the industrial application 
of aeration technology.
